analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare for America plan covering all residents with no deductibles, funded by higher taxes on wealth and health industries.
analysis.headline: Introduced on December 19, 2024, two weeks before the session ended, with one cosponsor; it was referred to six committees and never received a hearing or vote before Congress adjourned on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new public health insurance program called Medicare for America. Starting in 2026 it would open a government plan on the ACA exchanges, then from 2027 automatically enroll everyone — at birth, when they turn 65, and as they lose other coverage — in a program covering hospital care, doctors, drugs, dental, vision, hearing, home-based long-term care, and abortion. There would be no deductible, premiums would be zero or sliding-scale for lower and middle incomes, and yearly out-of-pocket costs would be capped at $3,500 per person. It would pay for this by letting the 2017 corporate tax cuts expire, adding a surtax on high incomes, taxing investment income, and adding new excise taxes on alcohol, tobacco, and sugary drinks. It would also negotiate or override drug prices and, from 2029, fold Medicare, then Medicaid and CHIP, into the new program while keeping regulated private Medicare Advantage-style plans as an option.
analysis.who_benefits: Nearly everyone without generous employer coverage. Uninsured people and anyone on the exchanges gets a public plan whose premiums are zero below 200% of poverty and capped at 8% of income above that. People on Medicare keep their current premiums but gain dental, vision, and hearing coverage. People with disabilities no longer wait 24 months for Medicare. Most patients pay no deductibles and face out-of-pocket caps of $3,500 per person or $5,000 per household, with zero for anyone under 200% of poverty and full coverage for pregnancy, emergencies, generic drugs, and children. States get federally paid higher rates for Medicaid providers during the transition, and student-loan relief goes to providers who join.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured, Medicare patients, and lower-income households

how_it_helps.text: Premiums would be zero for households under 200% of the federal poverty line and no household would pay more than 8% of monthly income, with federal subsidies on a sliding scale up to 600% of poverty.

The program would have no deductible, cap annual out-of-pocket costs at $3,500 for an individual and $5,000 for a household (indexed to medical inflation), with zero cost-sharing for children, pregnancy, emergencies, generic drugs, and people with serious or complex conditions.

Benefits would include dental, vision, hearing aids, home- and community-based long-term care, gender-confirming care, acupuncture, and abortion, with no prior authorization or step-therapy restrictions and no balance billing.
The 24-month waiting period for Medicare coverage after a disability would be eliminated, and Medicaid waiting lists would be addressed.

The bill phases in automatic enrollment starting in 2027, including newborns, current Medicare beneficiaries, and Members of Congress and their staff, who would be enrolled in the same program as everyone else.

analysis.who_pays: High-income households and corporations bear most of the cost: the 2017 tax law's individual and corporate cuts would sunset, a surtax would be added, the net investment income tax would be raised, and inherited-asset gains would be taxed. Employers lose the health-savings-account deduction and would face contribution or coverage requirements for large workforces. Drug makers face price negotiations with government licensing of their patents if they refuse, and a ban on direct-to-consumer advertising. Alcohol, tobacco, and sugary-drink companies face new excise taxes, whose costs are partly passed to consumers. Health insurers lose their individual-market, Medicaid, and duplicative-coverage business.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, corporations, drug makers, and insurers

drawbacks.text: The funding package relies on broad tax increases: letting the 2017 tax cuts expire, a new surtax, higher investment-income taxes, and new excise taxes on alcohol, tobacco, and sugared drinks, which raise prices for ordinary consumers of those products.

From 2029 no private insurer could sell coverage duplicating the public plan's benefits, so people who like their current private plan would eventually lose it, though regulated Medicare Advantage for America plans and employer plans remain available as options.

Transitioning Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP into a single new program between 2029 and 2033 is a massive administrative change, and small employers with more than 100 employees would eventually have to either maintain qualifying coverage or enroll workers in the new program.
The bill keeps private Medicare Advantage insurers in business inside the new program at 95% of public payment rates, locking in a private channel alongside the public plan rather than replacing it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for ordinary people are large and concrete — universal enrollment, no deductibles, hard out-of-pocket caps, drug price negotiation with patent overrides — and they come at a real cost that the bill puts mostly on high earners, corporations, and health industries, though excise taxes on alcohol, tobacco, and sugary drinks hit ordinary consumers too. The design is more gradual and insurer-friendly than single-payer alternatives, keeping Medicare Advantage plans and employer coverage in place, which preserves choice for people who like their coverage but also preserves private profit inside the public program. The transition over 2027-2033 is complex and would require sustained federal management.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with two weeks left in the session and referred to six committees, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Medicare for America Act of 2024 on December 19, 2024, for herself and Rep. Jan Schakowsky.
The same day, the bill was referred to six committees: Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, Education and the Workforce, and House Administration.
It had one cosponsor, a Democrat.
No committee took further action and no floor vote occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing ever came to a vote, private health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and high-income households continue under current law with no new taxes, price negotiations, or coverage mandates; the bill ends as a statement of support rather than law.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 19, 2024 and referred it to six committees.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Republican leadership and committee chairs
against.what_they_did: No committee scheduled a hearing or markup and no floor vote was ever brought up during the bill's two weeks in the chamber.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and sole cosponsor were both Democrats, and the bill sat with the Republican-controlled House majority, so no record shows how the chamber would have divided.

industries.note: The bill eliminates insurers' individual-market business when the ACA exchanges end in 2031, ends their Medicaid and CHIP roles, and bans selling duplicate coverage, but it locks in a private Medicare Advantage for America channel from 2029 paid at 95% of public rates. Insurers would rather keep the current system entirely, so their interest in the bill runs against the public's.

The government would negotiate prices for all drugs in the program and could license patents to generic makers if manufacturers refuse, with an interim cap at foreign benchmark prices; a review board would police excessive prices and direct-to-consumer advertising would be suspended. These provisions exist precisely to cut what patients and the government pay for drugs.

Rates would be set at least 110% of Medicare/Medicaid levels for hospital care, with federal payments covering the gap with Medicaid rates through 2031 and a 30% boost for primary care, and balance billing would be banned — but providers lose the ability to privately contract above program rates and outpatient hospital payments become site-neutral. Roughly speaking, safety-net and primary-care providers gain while higher-reimbursed providers take a payment cut.

The bill funds coverage by letting the 2017 tax cuts expire, adding a surtax, raising the net investment income tax, and changing how inherited-asset gains are taxed. This is the mirror image of who benefits from the current tax code.

industries.industry: Alcohol, tobacco, and sugary drink makers
industries.note: New excise taxes on tobacco, alcohol, and sugared drinks would raise their prices; the industry's cost is partly passed on to consumers who buy these products.

The bill repeals the excise tax on high-cost employer plans and shields small employers (under 100 employees or $2 million payroll) from mandatory contributions if they enroll workers, but it repeals the health-savings-account deduction and large employers would have to maintain qualifying coverage or channel workers into the new program.
The new Prescription Drug and Medical Device Review Board would have power to prohibit excessive prices for devices as well as drugs, cutting into current pricing power.
